Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and let $\F$ be a codimension one, $C^\infty$ foliation on $M$, with isolated singularities of Morse type. The study and classification of pairs $(M,\F)$ is a challenging (and difficult) problem. In this setting, a classical result due to Reeb \cite{Reeb} states that a manifold admitting a foliation with exactly two center-type singularities is a sphere. In particular this is true if the foliation is given by a function. Along these lines a result due to Eells and Kuiper \cite{Ku-Ee} classify manifolds having a real-valued function admitting exactly three non-degenerate singular points. In the present paper, we prove a generalization of the above mentioned results. To do this, we first describe the possible arrangements of pairs of singularities and the corresponding codimension one invariant sets, and then we give an elimination procedure for suitable center-saddle and some saddle-saddle configurations (of consecutive indices). In the second part, we investigate if other classical results, such as Haefliger and Novikov (Compact Leaf) theorems, proved for regular foliations, still hold true in presence of singularities. At this purpose, in the singular set, $Sing(\F)$ of the foliation $\F$, we consider {\em{weakly stable}} components, that we define as those components admitting a neighborhood where all leaves are compact. If $Sing(\F)$ admits only weakly stable components, given by smoothly embedded curves diffeomorphic to $S^1$, we are able to extend Haefliger's theorem. Finally, the existence of a closed curve, transverse to the foliation, leads us to state a Novikov-type result.

Let \(M\) be a smooth manifold, and let \(\mathcal{F}\) be a codimension-one \(C^\infty\) foliation on \(M\) with isolated singularities of Morse type. The study and classification of pairs \((M,\mathcal{F})\) is a challenging and difficult problem. In this setting, a classical result due to Reeb \cite{Reeb} states that any manifold admitting a foliation with exactly two center-type singularities is a sphere. In particular, this holds when the foliation is defined by a function. Along similar lines, a result of Eells and Kuiper \cite{Ku-Ee} classifies manifolds admitting a real-valued function with exactly three non-degenerate singular points.

In the present paper, we prove a generalization of the aforementioned results. To this end, we first describe the possible arrangements of pairs of singularities and the corresponding codimension-one invariant sets. We then provide an elimination procedure for suitable center-saddle configurations, as well as for certain saddle-saddle configurations of consecutive indices.

In the second part of the paper, we investigate whether other classical results—such as the theorems of Haefliger and Novikov on compact leaves, originally proved for regular foliations—remain valid in the presence of singularities. For this purpose, within the singular set \(\operatorname{Sing}(\mathcal{F})\) of the foliation \(\mathcal{F}\), we consider \emph{weakly stable} components, defined as those components admitting a neighborhood in which all leaves are compact. If \(\operatorname{Sing}(\mathcal{F})\) consists only of weakly stable components given by smoothly embedded curves diffeomorphic to \(S^1\), we are able to extend Haefliger’s theorem. Finally, the existence of a closed curve transverse to the foliation leads us to formulate a Novikov-type result.

Let \(M\) be a smooth manifold, and let \(\F\) denote a \(C^\infty\), codimension-one foliation on \(M\) whose singularities are isolated and of Morse type. Understanding and classifying such pairs \((M,\F)\) is a hard and subtle problem. In this context, a classical theorem of Reeb \cite{Reeb} asserts that if a manifold carries a foliation with precisely two singularities of center type, then the manifold must be a sphere. This conclusion applies, in particular, when the foliation is defined by a function. In a related direction, Eells and Kuiper \cite{Ku-Ee} classified manifolds that admit a real-valued function with exactly three non-degenerate critical points.

In this paper, we establish a generalization of these results. Our approach begins by describing the possible configurations of pairs of singularities together with the associated codimension-one invariant sets. We then present a method for eliminating certain center-saddle configurations, as well as some saddle-saddle configurations whose indices are consecutive.

In the second part of the paper, we examine whether other classical theorems for regular foliations, such as the compact leaf theorems of Haefliger and Novikov, remain valid when singularities are allowed. For this purpose, within the singular set \(Sing(\F)\) of the foliation \(\F\), we introduce the notion of \emph{weakly stable} components: these are components that possess a neighborhood in which every leaf is compact. When all components of \(Sing(\F)\) are weakly stable and are given by smoothly embedded curves diffeomorphic to \(S^1\), we prove an extension of Haefliger’s theorem. Finally, the presence of a closed curve transverse to the foliation allows us to formulate a Novikov-type theorem.

Reeb’s classical theorem is a foundational result in the theory of foliations. It states that if a compact manifold admits a codimension one foliation with exactly two singularities, both of center type, then the manifold is homeomorphic to a sphere. This result connects the global topology of a manifold with the local behavior of a singular foliation, showing that a very restricted singular structure forces the manifold to have the simplest possible global form.

The paper under discussion generalizes this classical theorem, as well as related results of Eells and Kuiper concerning manifolds that admit functions with only a small number of non-degenerate critical points. In particular, the authors study codimension one foliations with isolated Morse-type singularities and investigate how the number and type of these singularities constrain the topology of the underlying manifold. Their work extends the classical picture from foliations with only center-type singularities to more general configurations involving both centers and saddles.

A central part of the paper is the description of possible arrangements of pairs of singularities and the codimension one invariant sets associated with them. These invariant sets arise naturally from the leaves of the foliation and from the separatrices of saddle singularities. By analyzing how such sets connect or separate singular points, the authors obtain a detailed picture of the possible global configurations of the foliation. This classification is essential for understanding when certain singularities can be simplified or removed.

The paper also develops elimination procedures for suitable configurations of singularities. In particular, the authors show how a center and a saddle can sometimes be eliminated together when they form an appropriate local or semi-local configuration. They also treat certain saddle-saddle configurations, especially when the saddles have consecutive Morse indices. These elimination results are analogous in spirit to cancellation theorems in Morse theory: under suitable geometric and dynamical conditions, pairs of singularities can be removed without changing the foliation outside a controlled region.

Finally, the authors extend important global theorems in foliation theory. They prove a version of Haefliger’s theorem under weaker stability assumptions on singular components, broadening the range of situations in which one can exclude certain types of transverse structures. They also formulate a Novikov-type result, showing that the existence of a closed transverse curve has strong consequences for the foliation, such as the presence of particular compact or invariant structures. Together, these results deepen the connection between singular foliation theory, Morse theory, and the topology of manifolds.

The paper is devoted to the study of codimension-one smooth foliations on manifolds that are allowed to have isolated singularities of Morse type. In the classical nonsingular theory, foliations are locally described by regular level sets of submersions, and much of their global behavior is controlled by the existence of compact leaves, holonomy, and transverse curves. In the singular setting considered here, the foliation is regular away from a discrete set of points, while near each singular point it is modeled on the level sets of a Morse function. Thus the singularities are divided into centers and saddles according to the index of the corresponding quadratic form.

A central goal of the paper is to extend classical theorems of Reeb and Eells–Kuiper to this broader context. Reeb’s stability and global stability phenomena show that compact leaves with suitable holonomy conditions can force a foliation to have a rigid global structure. Eells–Kuiper-type results, on the other hand, relate the existence of Morse functions with very few critical points to strong restrictions on the topology of the ambient manifold. The paper investigates how these ideas persist when a codimension-one foliation has finitely many isolated Morse singularities rather than arising from an everywhere regular fibration.

The authors analyze in detail the possible configurations of singularities and the invariant sets associated with them. Particular attention is given to the way regular leaves accumulate on singular points and to how centers and saddles can be connected through separatrices or singular components. The study distinguishes between local behavior near a singularity and global constraints imposed by the surrounding foliation. Centers behave like local extrema of a Morse function, being surrounded by compact leaves that are topologically spheres or sphere bundles in the local model. Saddles, by contrast, may create separatrices and branching behavior, making the global structure more complicated.

One important theme is the elimination of certain pairs of singularities. Under suitable geometric and dynamical hypotheses, a center-saddle pair can be removed by modifying the foliation in a controlled region, in analogy with the cancellation of critical points in Morse theory. The paper also considers elimination procedures for appropriate saddle-saddle pairs. These operations simplify the singular foliation while preserving the essential behavior outside the chosen neighborhood. By repeatedly applying such procedures when possible, one can reduce the foliation to a simpler form and obtain classification results for the original manifold and foliation.

The classification results obtained in the paper broaden the scope of the classical theorems. In favorable cases, the presence of only centers, or of centers together with controlled saddle configurations, forces the ambient manifold to have a highly restricted topology. For example, the manifold may be shown to be homeomorphic or diffeomorphic to a sphere, a projective space, or another space appearing in the Eells–Kuiper classification, depending on the number and type of singularities and on the topology of the leaves. The results show that even though singularities introduce new phenomena, Morse-type singularities still retain enough structure to permit strong global conclusions.

The paper also extends compact leaf theorems of Haefliger and Novikov to the singular setting. In the classical theory, the existence of certain transverse closed curves or compact leaves can force the appearance of compact leaves elsewhere, constrain the holonomy, or imply topological restrictions on the ambient manifold. The authors prove analogous results for singular foliations under suitable assumptions. In particular, they show that weakly stable singular components behave in many respects like stable compact leaves. Their presence can impose strong restrictions on nearby leaves and on the global topology of the foliation.

A further contribution is the analysis of transverse closed curves in manifolds with singular foliations. In nonsingular codimension-one foliation theory, such curves play a crucial role in results of Haefliger and Novikov, often signaling nontrivial recurrence or forcing compact leaves under appropriate hypotheses. The paper demonstrates that similar mechanisms survive in the Morse-singular case. Even though a transverse curve must avoid the singular set, its existence can interact with the singular components and invariant sets in a way that forces compactness or produces contradictions with certain global configurations.

Overall, the paper shows that many foundational principles of codimension-one foliation theory remain valid, in suitably modified form, when isolated Morse-type singularities are allowed. By combining local Morse-theoretic models, global foliation techniques, stability arguments, and singularity elimination methods, it develops a framework for understanding how centers, saddles, compact leaves, and transverse curves determine the topology of the ambient manifold. The results generalize classical theorems of Reeb, Eells–Kuiper, Haefliger, and Novikov, and they provide new classification and compactness theorems for singular codimension-one foliations.

**Let the Morse Code Speak**

Let us imagine a world before instant messages, emails, and smartphones—a world where communication across great distances depended on sound, rhythm, and patience. In that world, **Morse code** became one of the most important tools for sending messages quickly and reliably.

Morse code uses combinations of short and long signals, known as dots and dashes, to represent letters and numbers. The famous distress signal **SOS** is written as `... --- ...`, a simple pattern that has saved many lives at sea and in emergencies.

The invention of Morse code changed communication forever. It allowed people to send messages over telegraph wires, across oceans, and eventually through radio waves. Although modern technology has mostly replaced it, Morse code is still remembered as a powerful symbol of human creativity and connection.

Let the simple rhythm of dots and dashes remind us that even the smallest signals can carry great meaning.

Building on Reeb’s local and global stability phenomena, we analyze the structure of the singular set and its interaction with the regular leaves, with particular emphasis on weakly stable singular components. We show that, under natural stability and compactness hypotheses, the topology of \(M\) is strongly constrained by the indices of the Morse singularities and by the holonomy of adjacent regular leaves.

A central result is a Novikov-type theorem for singular codimension one foliations: the existence of a compact leaf with suitable transverse behavior, or equivalently of a weakly stable singular component satisfying a finite holonomy condition, forces the appearance of a Reeb-type component in the complement of the singular set. This provides an obstruction to the existence of foliations without generalized Reeb components and yields a decomposition of \(M\) into elementary foliated pieces determined by the singular strata.

We further relate the resulting classification to the Eells–Kuiper theory of manifolds admitting Morse functions with few critical points. In the extremal case where the foliation is defined by a closed Morse form or by the level sets of a Morse function with minimal critical data, the ambient manifold is shown to belong to the corresponding Eells–Kuiper list, including spheres, projective planes over the classical division algebras, and their smooth analogues in the appropriate dimensions. The classification obtained here thus interpolates between Reeb’s sphere theorem, Novikov’s compact leaf theory, and the Eells–Kuiper classification of exceptional Morse manifolds, providing a unified framework for codimension one foliations with Morse singularities.

We study smooth foliations on compact manifolds whose singular locus consists of center-type components and saddle-type components, with emphasis on the case in which the singular components are weakly stable embedded circles. We describe the local and global organization of the foliation near such components and prove structural results for the arrangement of center–saddle pairs. A central result is a cancellation theorem for saddle components of consecutive Morse indices. Under suitable compatibility and stability hypotheses, a pair of adjacent saddle components of indices \(r\) and \(r+1\) can be eliminated by a deformation of the foliation, preserving the ambient topology away from a controlled neighborhood of the pair. This provides a singular-foliation analogue of classical Morse cancellation and yields simplified normal forms for the global configuration of singularities.

As applications, we obtain extensions of the theorems of Haefliger and Novikov to foliations with non-isolated singularities. When the singular components are weakly stable embedded circles, the existence of certain compact leaves or invariant separating hypersurfaces forces strong global restrictions: in particular, the foliation admits closed invariant codimension-one sets and, under appropriate hypotheses, Reeb-type components or compact leaves analogous to those appearing in the nonsingular theory. These results show that many classical mechanisms governing codimension-one foliations persist in the presence of controlled center and saddle singularities, provided the singular circles satisfy weak stability and the center–saddle arrangement is compatible with the induced invariant stratification.

We study \(C^\infty\) codimension-one foliations with isolated Morse-type singularities on compact smooth manifolds. Such foliations arise naturally as level-set foliations of Morse functions, but the global topology of the ambient manifold is strongly constrained by the type and number of singularities and by the behavior of the regular leaves. Building on the classical stability ideas of Reeb \(\cite{Reeb}\) and subsequent developments in the theory of singular foliations, we analyze the case in which the singular set consists of centers and saddles.

A central result is the following sphere theorem: if a compact connected \(m\)-manifold \(M\), \(m\geq 3\), admits a \(C^\infty\) codimension-one foliation with precisely two center singularities and no saddle singularities, then \(M\) is homeomorphic, and under the usual smooth hypotheses diffeomorphic, to the sphere \(S^m\). In this situation the foliation is topologically equivalent to the standard foliation of \(S^m\) by concentric \((m-1)\)-spheres together with the two singular center leaves. This recovers the classical Reeb-type phenomenon: the presence of two stable center singularities forces the global manifold topology to be spherical.

More generally, when the foliation has centers together with saddle singularities, the topology of \(M\) depends on how separatrices and compact leaves organize the foliation. The existence of a compact regular leaf often produces a Reeb-stability neighborhood, yielding a saturated product region and strong restrictions on nearby leaves. In favorable cases, compactness of all leaves or the absence of saddle connections allows one to reduce the global structure to a finite decomposition into canonical foliated blocks. These decompositions relate the number and indices of Morse singularities to the topology of \(M\), in the spirit of Morse theory and singular foliation theory.

We also discuss extensions involving transverse closed curves. A transverse closed curve intersecting the foliation away from the singular set can obstruct global triviality and may force the existence of noncompact leaves, holonomy phenomena, or additional singular behavior. Conversely, under compact-leaf hypotheses, the absence of such transverse cycles can imply strong global stability and lead to classification results. These considerations connect the local Morse normal form near singularities with global questions about holonomy, leaf compactness, and the topology of the ambient manifold.

The results fit into a broader program comparing singular foliations with Morse functions and studying when local stability data determine global topology. In particular, the two-center case is closely related to the classical characterization of spheres, while more refined cases involving saddle singularities echo the topology of exceptional manifolds and the Eells–Kuiper type phenomena \(\cite{Ku-Ee}\). Thus codimension-one foliations with Morse singularities provide a geometric framework linking Reeb stability, Morse theory, compact-leaf decompositions, and sphere-recognition results.
